faq.a: It helps separate volume‑depletion (prerenal) from intrinsic renal injury; a ratio > 20 points to hypovolaemia.
faq.q: Why is the BUN/Cr ratio useful in children?

faq.a: No; early renal injury may have normal BUN, especially if creatinine is also low from low muscle mass.
faq.q: Can a normal BUN rule out renal disease?

faq.a: Measure serum urea (mmol/L) and multiply by 0.466 to approximate BUN; interpret with the same thresholds.
faq.q: What if the laboratory cannot measure BUN?

exam: A 4‑year‑old with severe malaria presents with dry mucosa and BUN = 45 mg/dL. What is your next step? — Assess volume status, start IV rehydration, and repeat BUN after 24 h.
A child with sickle‑cell disease has BUN = 30 mg/dL, creatinine = 0.6 mg/dL. How do you interpret the ratio? — BUN/Cr ≈ 50 suggests prerenal azotemia; look for dehydration or vaso‑occlusive crisis.
Why is BUN often higher than creatinine in dehydration but not in intrinsic renal failure? — Dehydration increases urea reabsorption in the proximal tubule, raising BUN disproportionately.

A patient on traditional herbal medicine has BUN = 70 mg/dL and granular casts. What is the likely pathology? — Intrinsic acute tubular necrosis from nephrotoxic herbs; stop the herb and monitor renal function.
How would you differentiate prerenal azotemia from early chronic kidney disease when BUN is mildly elevated? — Use BUN/Cr ratio, urine specific gravity, and presence of proteinuria or casts.
What red‑flag laboratory value mandates urgent referral for dialysis in a paediatric patient? — BUN > 100 mg/dL with oliguria or refractory metabolic acidosis.
Explain why NSAIDs should be avoided in a child with elevated BUN and suspected intrinsic renal injury. — NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin‑mediated renal blood flow, worsening ischemic injury.
A child with severe diarrhoea has BUN = 22 mg/dL, creatinine = 0.4 mg/dL. Is this concerning? — Ratio ≈ 55 indicates significant volume depletion; aggressive rehydration is required.
ai.title: Blood Urea Nitrogen in Children
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: BUN reflects renal handling of nitrogen waste and volume status. In low‑resource settings it guides assessment of dehydration, renal dysfunction and catabolic illness. Interpretation must consider age‑specific norms and common tropical diseases.

b: Normal paediatric range: 5–18 mg/dL (infants), 7–20 mg/dL (older children).
Elevated BUN suggests reduced renal clearance, increased production, or hypovolaemia.
sections.p: Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) measures the concentration of nitrogen from urea in serum, expressed in mg/dL. It is derived from total urea by multiplying BUN by 2.14.

b: BUN/Cr > 20 : prerenal azotemia (dehydration, heart failure).
BUN/Cr ≈ 10‑15 : intrinsic renal disease.
sections.p: BUN alone does not stage disease, but when combined with creatinine (BUN/Cr ratio) it helps differentiate prerenal from intrinsic renal injury.

b: Prerenal: diarrhoea, vomiting, malaria‑induced dehydration, severe burns, sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusive crisis.
Renal: acute tubular necrosis from sepsis, nephrotoxic herbal remedies, severe malaria, HIV‑associated nephropathy.
Post‑renal: obstructive uropathy from posterior urethral valves, schistosomal fibrosis.
sections.p: In East African children the most frequent precipitants are volume loss and catabolic infections.

b: Dehydration: dry mucous membranes, sunken fontanelle, tachycardia, poor skin turgor.
Renal failure: oliguria, peripheral oedema, hypertension, uremic encephalopathy (lethargy, irritability).
sections.p: Elevated BUN is a laboratory finding; the child may show signs of the underlying cause rather than a specific BUN symptom.

t.b: Is the azotemia prerenal or intrinsic? A ratio > 20 suggests hypovolaemia; a ratio ≈ 10‑15 suggests intrinsic renal injury.
Are there casts, protein or haematuria indicating intrinsic renal disease? Presence of granular casts supports ATN.
Is there accompanying metabolic acidosis or hyperkalaemia that may need urgent correction?
Does the kidney size or bladder volume suggest obstruction or chronic disease?

t.a: If BUN is unavailable, use serum urea (mmol/L) and multiply by 0.466 to approximate BUN.
t.b: Provides a comparable value when the standard BUN assay is not on site.

b: BUN > 100 mg/dL with oliguria → consider dialysis.
Rapid rise in BUN with worsening mental status → uremic encephalopathy.
Persistent BUN/Cr > 20 despite rehydration → look for intrinsic renal damage.
sections.p: Severe azotemia can progress to uremia, fluid overload, and life‑threatening electrolyte disturbances.

b: Rehydration: oral rehydration solution or IV isotonic fluids (0.9 % saline) for prerenal azotemia.
Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (e.g., NSAIDs, aminoglycosides) unless essential.
If intrinsic renal failure suspected, stop offending agents, monitor urine output, consider referral for dialysis.
Correct acidosis with bicarbonate only if pH < 7.2 and patient symptomatic.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; then correct volume, electrolytes and acid‑base status.

b: Educate caregivers on early rehydration for diarrhoea and malaria.
Screen children with sickle cell disease for renal dysfunction annually.
Promote safe herbal‑medicine practices; avoid unregulated nephrotoxins.
sections.p: Repeat BUN/Cr after 24 h of fluid therapy; monitor urine output and weight.

b: Serum urea is the total urea concentration; BUN is the nitrogen component (BUN = urea × 2.14).
Creatinine clearance estimates GFR; BUN alone does not reflect filtration rate.
sections.p: BUN is sometimes mistaken for serum urea or for creatinine clearance.

b: High‑protein diet or catabolic states (e.g., severe infection) raise BUN without renal injury.
Corticosteroid therapy increases protein catabolism, elevating BUN.
Low muscle mass in malnourished children can keep creatinine low, falsely exaggerating BUN/Cr ratio.
sections.p: Certain conditions alter BUN independently of renal function.

whenToSeekHelp: BUN > 100 mg/dL with oliguria or altered mental status
Rapidly rising BUN despite adequate fluids
Signs of uremic pericarditis (chest pain, friction rub) or severe metabolic acidosis
